title: USS George Washington Headed to Middle East to Replace Strained Abraham Lincoln
excerpt: The U.S. Navy is rotating in a fresh aircraft carrier as lawmakers raise alarm over deteriorating conditions and mental health crises aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln after more than 250 days at sea.
body:
• The USS George Washington is heading to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln as part of a previously planned carrier rotation
  • The Lincoln has been deployed for over 250 days and has not made a port call in more than 200 days, setting a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea
  • Lawmakers are pressing the Pentagon over reports of water contamination, food shortages, deteriorating mental health, and at least one sailor going overboard
  • The Lincoln was redirected to the Middle East in January and has been central to Operation Epic Fury and the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports

A Record-Breaking Deployment Under Scrutiny

The U.S. Navy is preparing to send the aircraft carrier USS George Washington to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, according to U.S. officials familiar with the matter. The rotation comes as bipartisan lawmakers demand answers about alarming conditions aboard the Lincoln, which has been at sea longer than any U.S. carrier in modern history.

The Lincoln began a scheduled deployment from San Diego in November and was redirected to the Middle East in January ahead of the U.S. war against Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal. The carrier and its embarked aircraft were instrumental to Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. bombing campaign against Iran, and the ship has since participated in the blockade of Iranian ports.

"There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system."

— Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), in a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth

Sailors Under Strain

With more than 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard, the Lincoln has not made a port call in more than 200 days — a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea, according to Blumenthal, a member of the Armed Services Committee. The senator wrote to Hegseth and Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao on Wednesday expressing "serious concern" about the deployment.

CNN reported that a sailor went overboard from the Lincoln last month and was quickly rescued. Stars and Stripes and the Navy Times reported this week that there had been multiple attempts by crew members to jump overboard, citing interviews with sailors and families.

Around 200 family members attended town hall meetings in San Diego last Thursday to voice concerns to Acting Navy Secretary Cao and other senior officials. One spouse tearfully told officials she had received a message from her husband saying "he hopes he doesn't wake up tomorrow," according to Stars and Stripes.

Democratic Rep. Mike Levin of California said families described "moldy showers, broken toilets, no hot water for weeks, meals that came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas."

Rotation Was Previously Planned

The George Washington carrier group finished a port visit in Vietnam on August 5 and is currently headed to the Middle East, a U.S. official told CNN. The carrier rotation was planned before concerns were raised about living conditions, according to officials. It was not immediately clear when the Washington would arrive.

The U.S. Navy said in a statement to CNN: "We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise."

Broader Implications

The situation aboard the Lincoln reflects wider strain on the U.S. Navy, which has maintained an elevated carrier presence in the Middle East since the war with Iran began in February. The USS Gerald R. Ford earlier this year broke the record for the longest aircraft carrier deployment since the Vietnam War.

Rep. Seth Moulton, a Marine veteran on the House Armed Services Committee, told CNN his committee would investigate. "We have a president, a Commander-in-Chief, who’s made fun of troops for mental health issues. We have a secretary of defense who’s more focused on testosterone tests than actually keeping our troops alive," he said.

Blumenthal warned the Pentagon: "If the Administration intends to maintain a prolonged military campaign or an elevated carrier presence in the region, it must explain how it intends to ensure today’s operational requirements do not create tomorrow’s readiness crisis."
